Fidelity decay Sensitivity to small perturbations in system parameters is one of the most widely appreciated characteristics of quantum chaotic dynamics. This concept can be quantified via a variety of related signatures such as fidelity decay, Loschmidt amplitude and echo, and outof-time order correlators (OTOCs) [67, 52, 116, 117, 76], which are also useful in other contexts like quantum phase transitions and systems with broken time-reversal symmetries [116, 117, 76]. However, a drawback is that such signatures are reliable only if the perturbation itself does not show RMT distributions in its eigenvector statistics [52]. The main observation from the results in this section 2 is that, to observe XRMT ∼ 1, the cavity truncation dimension should be dimc ∼ dimj . Together with the behaviours of the dynamical quantities (discussed in the 2 main text and Appendix E.2), these XRMT results suggest that quantum chaotic dynamics in the Dicke DQS is mainly driven by the spin component. This is consistent with a simple intuition that the non-commutations in the Dicke DQS result from single qubit rotations that affect only the collective spin component. We nevertheless note the importance of developing a more theoretically rigorous understanding of these numerical results as an open question for further investigation. Observation of the RMT threshold in a truncated Hilbert space Figures 20 (a–c) show colour plots for 2 XRMT calculated as a function of both step size τ and cavity truncation dimension dimc , for three example spins j. These results firstly show that quantum chaotic dynamics in the Trotterised Dicke model, as illustrated by agreement with RMT statistics, emerge only after a threshold step size that appears to be largely independent of cavity truncation dimension as well as spin j. As this threshold is observable for a wide range of dimc / dimj ratios, across 1–2 orders of magnitude around dimc / dimj ∼ 1 for the spin sizes shown, this shows that the quantum chaotic dynamics are not an artefact that is highly sensitive to a particular choice of cavity dimension. Yet, across this range, as the 2 dimc used to analyse XRMT is increased, the extent of the quantum chaotic region beyond the threshold decreases. This supports the intuition that Trotter errors related to the spin-cavity interaction in the Dicke model drive quantum chaotic dynamics within a finite subspace of the full spin-cavity Hilbert space, with the size of the participating portion of the infinite-dimensional cavity Hilbert space increasing in proportion to the spin dimension dimj . Given 2 this interpretation, our aim when using XRMT in the rest of this paper is to analyse the extent to which Trotter errors are creating quantum chaotic dynamics within that finite domain of interest. To that end, our results in the rest of this section aim to identify an appropriate way to choose 2 dimc directly from dimj without looking at the XRMT values coming out of the analysis. Sensitivity to cavity truncation Next, we analyse 2 XRMT as a function of dimc for a range of j values at one step size before (τ = 0.002 (2πg −1 )) and one after (τ = 0.19 (2πg −1 )) the threshold. In this case, we determine the RMT fit dimension from the total dimension of the truncated system, i.e. dimf = 12 dimj × dimc (accounting for parity symmetry). Figure 20 (d) shows, for a larger selection of spin sizes than above, that the eigenvector statistics before the threshold do not agree with RMT for any value of j or dimc . In the quan- tum chaotic region beyond the threshold, however, we ob2 serve that XRMT ∼ 1 (with agreement defined by the shaded regions representing the 99% confidence regions for each system size) for cavity truncations in a region around dimc / dimj that becomes more sharply defined with increasing j (for the step size shown in Fig. 20 (e), 2 the XRMT ∼ 1 region appears to be asymptoting towards 0.3 ≲ dimc / dimj ≲ 5), before rapidly transitioning to 2 a region of large XRMT for larger truncations. Though we leave it as an open question to find a rigorous explanation, our results show that there is a relatively wide range of cavity truncations that give good agreement with RMT. 2 In Fig. 20 (f), we plot XRMT versus step size for various system sizes, with dimc = ⌈ 12 (dimj +1)⌉ = ⌈ 21 (2j + 2)⌉, showing results that are qualitatively the same as the main text, where we set dimc = dimj for the same spin values, with the same threshold position and overall behaviour, as 2 further illustration that our main results regarding XRMT for the Dicke model do not depend sensitively on dimc . Effective RMT dimension Having observed agreement with RMT for a region around dimc ∼ dimj in Figs 20 (a– c) and (e), we now fix the cavity truncation dimension to 2 dimc ∼ dimj and calculate XRMT for the same step size chosen in Fig. 20 (e), while varying the fit dimension dimf for various j values. Note, we choose dimc = dimj +1 = 2j +2, because that ensures that D = dimc × dimj is even, and this makes it easy to properly account for the Dicke model’s two-fold parity symmetry. (For the smallest case of j = 1/2, we instead choose dimc = dimj +4 = 6, because that gives a unitary that has enough components for 2 reliable XRMT analysis, even once parity symmetry elimi2 nates half of them, while still lying within the XRMT ∼1 region from Fig. 20 (e).) The results in Figure 20 (g) 2 confirm that XRMT ∼ 1 is observed only for dimf ∼ 1 dim × dim . Qualitatively similar shaped curves (not j c 2 shown) are observed for other choices of cavity truncation dimension dimc = k × dimj + mod(k × dim2j , 2) (dimc = ⌈k × dimj ⌉ + mod(dimj ×⌈k × dimj ⌉, 2) for k = 1/2), but the curves and their minima shift upwards as the cavity truncation increases. To explore the impact of the chosen dimc on the RMT fit dimension dimf , we plot the dimf which minimises 2 XRMT against spin j for k ranging between k = 0.5 and 2 k = 5 (Figure 20 (h))—and the minimum XRMT value reached at the optimal dimf (Figure 20 (i)). In Fig. 20 (h), we see that the optimised dimf closely follows the expected trend of dimf = 12 dimj × dimc , whenever the cavity truncation dimension is in the regime where the eigenvector statistics show agreement with RMT at the optiimised dimf . When this is not the case—that is, when the observed statistics do not agree with RMT statistics—it is probably not surprising that the dimf which minimises 2 doesn’t match the dimension of the truncated TrotXRMT terised unitary.
